claims.text: The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is an as-cast, single-phase BCC material.
The initial alloy is chemically disordered and has a homogeneous microstructure.
Large atomic-size mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr produces significant local lattice distortions.
Heating from about 673 K to 1073 K expands the locally distorted lattice nonuniformly.
Thermal expansion of the distorted lattice increases the energy barriers for edge-dislocation glide.
Dislocation migration is unusually slow in random and short-range-ordered HfNbTaTiZr.
The slow dislocation migration in HfNbTaTiZr is specifically caused by thermally enhanced edge-dislocation barriers.
Suppression of edge-dislocation motion counteracts ordinary thermal softening.
HfNbTaTiZr should display a yield-strength plateau between approximately 673 K and 1073 K.
The elastic moduli of HfNbTaTiZr should have anomalously weak temperature dependence between approximately 673 K and 1073 K.
Chemical short-range order makes HfNbTaTiZr stiffer and harder than its random-alloy counterpart.
Short-range order changes the dislocation plasticity, plastic-zone size, and dislocation density in HfNbTaTiZr.
Annealing can subtly promote short-range order in the tested HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Anneal-induced short-range order should produce a more pronounced strength plateau or greater elevated-temperature yield retention.
Diffraction should reveal moderate, isotropic lattice-strain changes during thermal expansion.
Conventional BCC alloys typically lose yield strength gradually with increasing temperature because of thermally activated dislocation glide.
Below roughly 673 K, standard elastic behavior should dominate over the proposed edge-dislocation barrier effect.
Above roughly 1073 K, dynamic recovery or phase instability may override the proposed edge-dislocation barrier effect.
An inert Ar/H2 atmosphere minimizes oxidation during elevated-temperature testing.
Yield-strength retention may vary with strain rate and minor compositional fluctuations.
